standard.title: Evaluate civic perspectives and interpretations
standard.description: analyse information, data and ideas about political, legal or civic issues to identify and evaluate differences in perspectives and interpretations
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can analyse information about civic issues to identify and explain differences in perspectives and potential challenges (AC9HC8S03). At Year 9 the expectation advances from explaining differences to evaluating them — students must assess the values, motivations and contexts that underpin perspectives, not just identify that perspectives differ.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse information about political, legal or civic issues to identify and evaluate differences in perspectives and interpretations, including examining the values and motivations underlying those perspectives.

nodes.label: Identifying values and motivations underlying perspectives
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the values, motivations and contexts that underpin different perspectives on a civic or political issue.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify the values or motivations underlying at least two different perspectives on a civic or political issue.
nodes.typical_width: Identify the values, motivations and contexts that underpin different perspectives about political and legal systems and processes; explain why the same information can be interpreted differently depending on perspective; apply this to at least one substantive civic issue (e.g. constitutional recognition for First Nations Australians, impacts of mining activity on communities).
wider: Investigate a civic issue where perspectives divide along lines of lived experience (e.g. First Nations Australians' perspectives on constitutional recognition versus non-Indigenous perspectives) and analyse how context shapes interpretation
Examine a historical civic issue and a contemporary one to compare whether the values underpinning key perspectives have changed over time
Map perspectives on a policy debate using a values framework (e.g. liberty, equality, community, authority) to evaluate what is really at stake in the disagreement
nodes.hinge_reason: If students can only identify that perspectives differ without understanding why, the evaluation in Node 2 is superficial — they end up comparing conclusions rather than reasoning. Evaluation requires understanding that perspectives are grounded in values and contexts, not just positions.

response_modes.reason: The move from 'these perspectives differ' to 'these perspectives differ because they prioritise different values' is the key analytical step. Students benefit from an explicit scaffold that asks: what does this perspective assume? What does it prioritise? What would challenge it?

success_criteria: Identifies at least two perspectives on a civic issue
Explains the value or motivation underlying each perspective, not just the position held

nodes.label: Evaluating effectiveness and policy responses
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate the effectiveness of a political or legal institution and examine how government responds to civic issues.
nodes.minimum_width: Examine at least one perspective on the effectiveness of a political or legal institution and explain the basis for that assessment.
nodes.typical_width: Examine information including diverse perspectives about the effectiveness of a political or legal institution (e.g. 'Is Australia's parliament representative of the Australian community?' or 'Does the court system deliver justice for victims of crime?'); investigate how the Australian Government responds to a civic issue and examine the policy development and implementation process; evaluate the quality of different perspectives using evidence.
wider: Investigate a government policy response to a major civic issue (e.g. welfare reform in response to economic crisis, health policy during COVID) and evaluate its effectiveness from multiple stakeholder perspectives
Examine a case where natural disaster or emergency response policy was evaluated differently by different communities (e.g. rural vs urban, First Nations vs non-Indigenous) and analyse why
Assess the effectiveness of a political institution (e.g. the Senate, an ombudsman office) using criteria drawn from multiple civic perspectives including those of underrepresented groups

response_modes.reason: Evaluation is stronger when students have multiple policy contexts to draw on. Using two contrasting cases — one where government response was broadly effective, one where it was contested or inadequate — develops evaluative flexibility.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Policy effectiveness evaluation is where civic analysis becomes genuinely critical — advancing students can assess institutional effectiveness against competing criteria (efficiency, equity, representation, responsiveness) using real and recent Australian cases.
success_criteria: Evaluates at least one perspective on the effectiveness of a political or legal institution using evidence
Examines a government response to a civic issue and identifies at least two different perspectives on its effectiveness
